@graph.headline: Crypto PR vs AI PR in 2026: how the playbooks differ
@graph.alternativeHeadline: A side-by-side teardown of the Web3 and AI startup PR playbooks
@graph.description: A 2026 side-by-side comparison of crypto PR and AI PR. Different outlets, different journalists, different proof requirements, different narrative arc, different measurement — and how to tell which playbook your startup actually needs.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between crypto PR and AI PR?

acceptedAnswer.text: Crypto PR and AI PR are two distinct playbooks. Crypto PR works through crypto-native outlets such as CoinDesk, Cointelegraph, The Block and Decrypt, runs on a fast news cycle pegged to launches and token events, leans on KOL and community channels, and operates under heavy regulatory caution around price and token claims. AI PR works through mainstream technology and business press such as Forbes, TechCrunch, The Information, Wired and AI Magazine, runs on a slower category-narrative cycle, leans on analyst relations and enterprise credibility, and has no token to manage. A startup that is both an AI company and a Web3 company usually needs both playbooks run in parallel, not one merged campaign.

mainEntity.name: Which outlets matter for crypto PR vs AI PR?

acceptedAnswer.text: For crypto PR, the Tier-1 set is CoinDesk, Cointelegraph, The Block, Decrypt, Blockworks and Bitcoin Magazine, with regional crypto outlets across Korea, Japan and India for APAC launches. For AI PR, the Tier-1 set is Forbes, TechCrunch, The Information, Wired, VentureBeat, MIT Technology Review and AI Magazine, plus business desks at Bloomberg and the Financial Times for enterprise stories. The journalists, the pitch norms and the proof they ask for are different on each side, which is why a crypto PR contact list does not transfer cleanly to an AI campaign.

mainEntity.name: Does an AI startup need crypto-style KOL marketing?

acceptedAnswer.text: Usually not in the same form. Crypto KOL marketing is a structured channel: vetted creators on X, Telegram and YouTube running coordinated campaigns around a token or launch, often with disclosure and performance tracking. AI startups rely more on credibility intermediaries — named researchers, analysts, respected technical voices, and enterprise customer references — than on paid creator waves. The AI equivalent of a KOL wave is a founder thought-leadership program: op-eds, podcasts, conference talks and analyst briefings that build category authority over months rather than amplifying a single launch moment.

mainEntity.name: Is AI PR more expensive than crypto PR?

acceptedAnswer.text: Scope for scope, the costs are broadly similar — a fractional senior operator runs $5,000 to $12,000 per month for either, and specialist agencies run $15,000 to $45,000 per month. The difference is where the budget goes. Crypto PR spends more on KOL coordination, regional translation and exchange or launch communications. AI PR spends more on long-form founder content, analyst relations and sustained thought-leadership programming. AI campaigns also tend to run on a longer time horizon because the buying cycle for enterprise AI is slower than the attention cycle in crypto.

mainEntity.name: Why can't a crypto PR campaign be reused for an AI launch?

acceptedAnswer.text: The two playbooks optimise for different things. A crypto campaign is built for speed, simultaneity and community velocity around a dated event. An AI campaign is built for credibility, depth and category narrative over a quarter or more. The crypto outlets, the embargo norms, the KOL channels and the price-sensitive language discipline do not map onto a TechCrunch or Information feature, which wants product substance, named enterprise customers, defensible technical claims and a founder who can articulate where the category is going. Reusing a crypto press kit for an AI launch typically reads as thin to a mainstream tech reporter.
